challenges.title: Label the AI-written reply?
challenges.scene: Your team now drafts replies to customers' personal concerns with AI, and legal wants an "AI-written" label. In an experiment, people described a situation and got a reply from Bing Chat or a person.
challenges.question: What does the experiment predict for labeled AI replies?
options: AI replies feel colder, label or not
AI replies feel more heard; the label erodes it
The AI label raises trust and feeling heard
Source and label make no difference

chart.note: Feeling heard, 7-point scale; source and label manipulated separately. Values reported in Yin, Jia & Wakslak 2024, Results.

challenges.answerTitle: AI helps people feel heard; the label undercuts it
challenges.explain: AI replies made people feel more heard than human replies (5.74 vs 5.17), but an AI label lowered feeling heard (5.13 vs 5.81 for a human label).
challenges.implication: Keep the label, but expect a dip; measure customers' attitudes toward AI and have staff personalize sensitive replies.
challenges.boundary: One online experiment with Bing Chat and one-off replies; long customer relationships were not studied.

follow.q: Was the AI better at reading emotions?
follow.a: Yes. Bing Chat was more accurate than human responders at detecting four of six basic emotions, with no difference for anger or surprise.

follow.q: Who did not mind the label?
follow.a: Recipients with very positive attitudes toward the AI showed no negative label effect.

follow.q: What about colleagues who use AI?
follow.a: A related PNAS study found people helped by AI are rated lazier, and employees expect this and hide AI use (Reif et al. 2025).
